title: How does the Servlet model handle concurrent requests, why doesn't one slow request block others, and why is storing per-request state in a singleton bean a bug?
shortTitle: Servlet concurrency — one thread per request, singleton thread safety, pool exhaustion

s1_definition.profdef: Spring MVC runs on a Servlet container (Tomcat default, 200 threads). Each HTTP request gets one thread from the pool for its entire lifecycle. Singleton beans are shared across ALL threads. Mutable instance fields in singletons create race conditions. Local variables are thread-safe (each thread has its own stack). Thread pool exhaustion occurs when slow downstream calls hold threads indefinitely — always set timeouts.
s1_definition.analogy: 200 teller windows at National Bank of India. Each customer gets one window. All tellers share ONE calculator (singleton). If teller A writes "50000" and teller B writes "75000" simultaneously, the result is corrupted. Each teller's personal notepad (local variables) is safe.
s1_definition.oneliner: One thread per request, 200 threads default. Singletons shared by ALL threads — no mutable instance fields. Always set timeouts on downstream calls.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring MVC runs on a Servlet container (Tomcat default, 200 threads). Each HTTP request gets one thread from the pool for its entire lifecycle. Singleton beans are shared across ALL threads. Mutable instance fields in singletons create race conditions. Local variables are thread-safe (each thread has its own stack). Thread pool exhaustion occurs when slow downstream calls hold threads indefinitely — always set timeouts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** 200 teller windows at National Bank of India. Each customer gets one window. All tellers share ONE calculator (singleton). If teller A writes "50000" and teller B writes "75000" simultaneously, the result is corrupted. Each teller's personal notepad (local variables) is safe.

**One line to remember:** One thread per request, 200 threads default. Singletons shared by ALL threads — no mutable instance fields. Always set timeouts on downstream calls.

sections.s2_technical:
**Thread-per-request:** Tomcat thread pool (default 200). Each request gets exclusive thread. Threads are independent — one slow request does not block others unless ALL 200 are busy.

**Singleton thread safety:** The SAME service instance serves all 200 threads. Injected `final` dependencies = safe (assigned once). Mutable instance fields = RACE CONDITION. Use local variables, `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicReference`, or request-scoped beans for per-request state.

**Pool exhaustion:** A downstream call with no timeout holds the thread indefinitely. At 10 req/s and 30s timeout-less calls, all 200 threads are blocked in 20 seconds. New requests queue, then timeout. Fix: set explicit timeout on EVERY downstream call.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's order matching engine has a singleton bean that tracks the "last matched order" in a mutable field.** Under load testing with 100 concurrent users, the logs show incorrect order details — customer A's log shows customer B's order. Also, the exchange price API has no timeout, causing thread pool exhaustion during exchange outages.

**What the project will show:** A thread-safe order matching service using ConcurrentHashMap, a demonstration of the race condition with mutable singleton state, proper timeout configuration on RestClient calls, and thread pool monitoring.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** BUY order arrives on Thread-1 (of 200). OrderMatchingService is a singleton — shared by all threads. But ALL mutable state is in local variables (orderId, threadName) or thread-safe structures (AtomicInteger, ConcurrentHashMap). No race conditions.

**Step 2.** Thread-1 saves the BUY order. Tries to find a matching SELL order with pessimistic lock (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`). No match found. Order queued as PENDING.

**Step 3.** SELL order arrives on Thread-2. Same singleton service. Thread-2's local variables are completely independent from Thread-1's. Finds the BUY order with pessimistic lock. Both orders marked as MATCHED. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() safely counts matches across all threads.

**Step 4.** If ExchangePriceService call times out (configured 5s read timeout in application.yml), the thread is released after 5 seconds. Without timeout, the thread would block indefinitely, contributing to pool exhaustion.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  200 Tomcat Threads (thread pool)
    │
    ├─ Thread-1: POST /orders {"side":"BUY","symbol":"RELIANCE","qty":100}
    │   ▼
    │  OrderMatchingService (SINGLETON — same instance for ALL threads)
    │   ├─ orderId = "ORD-A1B2" ← LOCAL variable (thread-safe, on Thread-1's stack)
    │   ├─ orderRepo.save(buyOrder)
    │   ├─ orderRepo.findMatchingOrder("RELIANCE","SELL",100,2450) → empty
    │   └─ Response: PENDING
    │
    ├─ Thread-2: POST /orders {"side":"SELL","symbol":"RELIANCE","qty":100}
    │   ▼
    │  OrderMatchingService (SAME singleton instance!)
    │   ├─ orderId = "ORD-C3D4" ← DIFFERENT local variable (Thread-2's stack)
    │   ├─ orderRepo.save(sellOrder)
    │   ├─ orderRepo.findMatchingOrder("RELIANCE","BUY",100,2450)
    │   │   └─ SELECT ... FOR UPDATE → found ORD-A1B2 (LOCKED)
    │   ├─ buyOrder.markMatched()
    │   ├─ sellOrder.markMatched()
    │   ├─ matchCount.incrementAndGet() → 1 (AtomicInteger — thread-safe)
    │   └─ Response: MATCHED with ORD-A1B2
    │
    ├─ Thread-3 through Thread-200: handling other requests independently
    │
    └─ ALL threads share: orderRepo (singleton), priceCache (ConcurrentHashMap),
       matchCount (AtomicInteger) — all THREAD-SAFE structures
       NEVER share: mutable instance fields like "private String lastOrderId"

  ═══ POOL EXHAUSTION SCENARIO ═══

  Without timeout:
    Thread-1: exchangeClient.getPrice() → exchange is DOWN → blocks FOREVER
    Thread-2: exchangeClient.getPrice() → blocks FOREVER
    ... 200 threads blocked → pool exhausted → new requests rejected → 503

  With timeout (exchange.read-timeout: 5s):
    Thread-1: exchangeClient.getPrice() → 5s → TimeoutException → thread freed
    → Circuit breaker opens → fallback to cached price → service stays alive ✅
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring MVC uses Tomcat's thread-per-request model with a default pool of 200 threads. Each request gets an exclusive thread for its entire lifecycle. Singleton beans are shared across all threads simultaneously, so they must be thread-safe. Final fields holding injected dependencies are safe because they are assigned once during construction. Mutable instance fields are the danger: writing per-request data to a singleton field creates a race condition where Thread A's data is overwritten by Thread B.

In my banking order matching engine, the OrderMatchingService is a singleton that handles hundreds of concurrent orders. All per-request state lives in local variables on each thread's stack. Shared mutable state uses thread-safe structures: ConcurrentHashMap for the price cache and AtomicInteger for the match counter. The order matching query uses pessimistic locking to prevent two threads from matching the same order simultaneously. We configure explicit connect and read timeouts on every downstream HTTP client in application.yml, because a downstream call without a timeout holds the Tomcat thread indefinitely, and at sufficient request rates this exhausts the entire pool, making the application unresponsive even though CPU is idle.
